chapter_approach.heading: How this chapter is taught
chapter_approach.intro: The chapter follows the book's order. One building with floors above and below the ground gives meaning to negative numbers, then the same lift, the number line and tokens are used to add and subtract any integers.

points.title: One lift, many ideas
points.text: Every new idea starts in Bela's lift or on a number line: a floor is a number, a button press is a movement, and Starting Floor + Movement = Target Floor.

points.title: Concept, then practice, topic by topic
points.text: Each idea gets its own topic: worked videos for the book's questions, a tool only where handling the lift, the line or the tokens is the idea, then the book's Figure it Out questions in a practice topic, each with its own video.

points.title: Why, not a trick
points.text: Signs are never handled by a memorised rule. A result such as 2 minus a negative is read off the lift, the number line or the tokens first, and the rule is named afterwards.

points.title: Keeko's doubts
points.text: The common wrong ideas, such as 'minus 4 is bigger than minus 3 because 4 is bigger than 3', are raised by Keeko and fixed with a floor, a line or a token, never just a rule.

design_references.text: maths6_ch9 new_design plan: framing intro with one hook, idea topics ending in one doer, optional tool where the manipulation is the idea, a practice topic after each idea topic with one video per book question, one summary topic.

modules.module_summary: Bela's Building of Fun has floors above and below the ground. Floor numbers, lift button presses, inverses and comparing floors give the first meaning of positive and negative numbers and of adding them.

concepts.concept_name: Can a number be less than zero?

content.text:
Recall that the very first numbers we learned about in the study of mathematics were the counting numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, ...
Then we learned that there are even more numbers! For example, there is the number 0 (zero), representing nothing, which comes before 1. The number 0 has a very important history in India and now in the world. For example, around the world we learn to write numbers in the Indian number system using the digits 0 to 9, allowing us to write numbers however large or however small using just these 10 digits.
We then learned about more numbers that exist between the numbers 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, ..., such as 1/2, 3/2, and 13/6. These are called fractions.
But are there still more numbers? Well, 0 is an additional number that we didn't know about earlier, and it comes before 1 and is less than 1. Are there perhaps more numbers that come before 0 and are less than 0?
Phrased another way, we have seen the number line:
However, this is actually only a number 'ray', in the language we learned earlier in geometry; this ray starts at 0 and goes forever to the right. Do there exist numbers to the left of 0, so that this number ray can be completed to a true number line?
That is what we will investigate in this chapter!
Can there be a number less than 0? Can you think of any ways to have less than 0 of something?

content.text:
1. Think first: the number ray starts at 0 and runs to the right. Can you think of a time when you had less than zero of something?
2. Counting numbers came first, then 0 before 1, then fractions between the numbers. Each time, the numbers grew by something new.
3. Now the question is the one on the other side of zero: is there a number that comes before 0 and is less than 0? That is what this chapter investigates.

content.text:
Children flock to Bela's ice cream factory to see and taste her tasty ice cream. To make it even more fun for them, Bela purchased a multi-storied building and filled it with attractions. She named it Bela's Building of Fun.
But this was no ordinary building!
Observe that some of the floors in the 'Building of Fun' are below the ground. What are the shops that you find on these floors? What is there on the ground floor?

content.text:
1. Think first: a building can go up, but can a floor go below the ground? What would you find there?
2. In Bela's Building of Fun, some floors are below the ground: a Toy Store, a Video Games shop, a Cinema, a Ghost House and a Dinosaur floor.
3. The ground floor is the Welcome Hall. So there are places that are not above the start but below it, and we need numbers for them.

content.text:
A lift is used to go up and down between the floors. It has two buttons: '+' to go up and '−' to go down. Can you spot the lift?
To go to the Art Centre from the 'Welcome Hall', you must press the '+' button twice.
We say that the button press is + + or +2.
To go down two floors, you must press the '−' button twice, which we write as − − or −2.
So if you press +1 (i.e., if you press the '+' button once), then you will go up one floor and if you press −1 (i.e., if you press the '−' button once), then you will go down 1 floor.
Lift button presses and numbers: +++ is written as +3; − − − − is written as −4.
What do you press to go four floors up? What do you press to go three floors down?

content.text:
1. Think first: the lift has two buttons, '+' and '−'. If you press '+' four times, what single number could stand for that?
2. Each '+' press takes you up one floor and each '−' press takes you down one floor. Four '+' presses are written +4, and three '−' presses are written −3.
3. So a button press is a number with a direction: the sign says up or down, and the number says how many floors.

content.text:
Entry to the 'Building of Fun' is at the ground floor level and is called the 'Welcome Hall'. Starting from the ground floor, you can reach the Food Court by pressing +1 and can reach the Art Centre by pressing +2. So, we can say that the Food Court is on Floor +1 and that the Art Centre is on Floor +2.
Starting from the ground floor, you must press −1 to reach the Toy Store. So, the Toy Store is on Floor −1 similarly starting from the ground floor, you must press −2 to reach the Video Games shop. So, the Video Games shop is on Floor −2.
The ground floor is called Floor 0. Can you see why?
Number all the floors in the Building of Fun.
Did you notice that +3 is the floor number of the Book Store, but it is also the number of floors you move when you press +3? Similarly, −3 is the floor number but it is also the number of floors you go down when you press −3, i.e., when you press − − −.
A number with a '+' sign in front is called a positive number. A number with a '−' sign in front is called a negative number.
In the 'Building of Fun', the floors are numbered using the ground floor, Floor 0, as a reference or starting point. The floors above the ground floor are numbered with positive numbers. To get to them from the ground floor, one must press the '+' button some number of times. The floors below the ground are numbered with negative numbers. To get to them from the ground floor, one must press the '−' button some number of times.
Zero is neither a positive nor a negative number. We do not put a '+' or '−' sign in front of it.

content.text:
1. Think first: if the Food Court is one press of '+' from the ground floor, what number would you give it? What about the Toy Store, one press of '−' down?
2. The Food Court is Floor +1 and the Toy Store is Floor −1. A number with a '+' sign is positive and a number with a '−' sign is negative.
3. The ground floor is the reference point. No button is needed to be there, so it is Floor 0, and zero is neither positive nor negative.

media.title: Why is the ground floor called Floor 0?
media.context: The Other Side of Zero. Concept video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea. It ends when Keeko raises a hand with a doubt. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: Each floor number tells how many button presses reach it from the ground floor. The ground floor needs no press at all, and that count gives its number. Keeko thinks the ground floor should be floor one because counting starts from one, and the count of presses breaks that doubt.

content.text:
Start from the Food Court and press +2 in the lift. Where will you reach? ____________
We can describe this using an expression: Starting Floor + Movement = Target Floor.
The starting floor is +1 (Food Court) and the number of button presses is +2. Therefore, you reach the target floor (+1) + (+2) = +3 (Book Store).

content.text:
Gurmit was in the Toy Store and wanted to go down two floors. But by mistake he pressed the '+' button two times. He realised his mistake and quickly pressed the '−' button three times. How many floors below or above the Toy Store will Gurmit reach?
Gurmit will go one floor down. We can show the movement resulting from combining button presses as an expression: (+2) + (−3) = −1.

content.text:
1. Think first: Gurmit presses '+' twice by mistake, then '−' three times. Does he end up above or below where he began?
2. The two movements are +2 and −3, and combining them is the addition (+2) + (−3) = −1.
3. So combining button presses is also addition, and he ends one floor below the Toy Store.

content.text:
On the ground floor, Basant is in a great hurry and by mistake he presses +3. What can he do to cancel it and stay on the ground floor? He can cancel it by pressing −3. That is, (+3) + (−3) = 0.
We call −3 the inverse of +3. Similarly, the inverse of −3 is +3.
If Basant now presses +4 and then presses −4 in the lift, where will he reach?
Here is another way to think of the concept of inverse. If you are at Floor +4 and you press its inverse −4, then you are back to zero, the ground floor! If you are at Floor −2 and you press its inverse +2, then you go to (−2) + (+2) = 0, again the ground floor!
Write the inverses of these numbers: +4, −4, −3, 0, +2, −1.
Connect the inverses by drawing lines.

media.title: What is the inverse of each number?
media.context: The Other Side of Zero. Concept video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea. It ends when Keeko raises a hand with a doubt. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: Two presses that bring the lift back to the start are called inverses, and a number and its inverse add up to zero. The inverse of each of the six given numbers is found by asking which press brings the lift back. Keeko thinks zero has no inverse because there is nothing to cancel, and zero added to zero breaks that doubt.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: the inverse of a number is the number that adds to it to give zero. Watch for students who think zero has no inverse.
media.instructions_for_student: When the video says think and tell, say your answer out loud. Then watch how the book's example is solved.

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students write a move in the lift as Starting Floor + Movement = Target Floor, and find the target floor.
Students combine a run of '+' and '−' presses into one movement and write it as an addition.
Students cancel a press with the press of equal size in the other direction, and name the inverse of an integer.
Students press lift buttons from different floors, read the target floor and write the addition.

content.text:
10.1, page 4, Figure it Out 3: Starting from different floors, find the movements required to reach Floor −5. For example, if I start at Floor +2, I must press −7 to reach Floor −5. The expression is (+2) + (−7) = −5. Find more such starting positions and the movements needed to reach Floor −5 and write the expressions.
1. Starting floor + movement = −5, so movement = −5 − starting floor.
Answer: Open-ended. Examples: (+1) + (−6) = −5; (−2) + (−3) = −5; 0 + (−5) = −5.

content.text:
10.1, page 6, Figure it Out 3: If Floor A = −12, Floor D = −1 and Floor E = +1 in the building shown on the right as a line, find the numbers of Floors B, C, F, G, and H.
1. A is −12 and D is −1, 11 ticks above A; B is 3 ticks above A, so −9; C is 6 ticks above A, so −6.
2. E = +1; F is one above, +2; G = +6; H = +11 (counted on the ticks).
Answer: B = −9, C = −6, F = +2, G = +6, H = +11.

concepts.concept_name: Subtraction as the missing number to add

content.text:
In earlier classes, we understood the meaning of subtraction as 'take away'. For example, there are 10 books on the shelf. I take away 4 books. How many are left on the shelf?
We can express the answer using subtraction: 10 − 4 = 6 or 'Ten take away four is six.'
You may also be familiar with another meaning of subtraction which is related to comparison or making quantities equal. For example, consider this situation: I have ₹10 with me and my sister has ₹6.
Now, I can ask the question: 'How much more money should my sister get in order to have the same amount as me?'
We can write this in two ways: 6 + ? = 10 Or 10 − 6 = ?
Here, we see the connection between 'finding the missing number to be added' and subtraction.
For subtraction of positive and negative numbers, we will use this meaning of subtraction as 'making equal' or 'finding the missing number to be added'.
Evaluate 15 − 5, 100 − 10 and 74 − 34 from this perspective.

Worked example: Evaluate 15 − 5, 100 − 10 and 74 − 34 from this perspective (subtraction as 'making equal' or 'finding the missing number to be added'). a) 15 − 5: 5 + ? = 15 b) 100 − 10: 10 + ? = 100 c) 74 − 34: 34 + ? = 74
Answer: 15 − 5 = 10, 100 − 10 = 90, 74 − 34 = 40.

content.text:
Teacher's Note: In general, when there are two unequal quantities, subtraction can indicate the change needed to make the quantities equal. Subtraction shows how much the starting quantity should change in order to become the target quantity. In the context of different floor levels, what is the change required to reach the Target Floor from the Starting Floor? Notice that the change needed may be positive (for an increase) or negative (for a decrease).
Your starting floor is the Art Centre and your target floor is the Sports Centre. What should be your button press?
You need to go three floors up, so you should press +3. We can write this as an expression using subtraction: Target Floor − Starting Floor = Movement needed.
In the above example, the starting floor is +2 (Art Centre) and the target floor is +5. The button press to get to +5 from +2 is +3. Therefore, (+5) − (+2) = +3
Explanation: Recall the connection between addition and subtraction. For 3 + ? = 5, we can find the missing number using subtraction: 5 − 3 = 2. That is, subtraction is the same as finding the missing number to be added.
We know that Starting Floor + Movement needed = Target Floor
If the movement needed is to be found, then, Starting Floor + ? = Target Floor. So, Target Floor − Starting Floor = ? = Movement needed

concepts.concept_name: Subtracting when floors are below the ground

content.text:
More examples:
a. If the Target Floor is −1 and Starting Floor is −2, what button should you press? You need to go one floor up, so, you should press +1. Expression: (−1) − (−2) = (+1)
b. If the Target Floor is −1 and Starting floor is +3, what button should you press? You need to go four floors down, so, you should press −4. Expression: (−1) − (+3) = (−4)
c. If the Target Floor is +2 and Starting Floor is −2, what button should you press? You need to go four floors up, so, you should press +4. Expression: (+2) − (−2) = (+4)

content.text:
1. Think first: you start on Floor −2 and want Floor −1. Is the movement up or down?
2. One floor up, so (−1) − (−2) = +1. From Floor +3 to Floor −1 you go four floors down, so (−1) − (+3) = −4. From Floor −2 to Floor +2 you go four floors up, so (+2) − (−2) = +4.
3. Read the movement off the lift, then write the subtraction. Taking away a negative start sends you up.

media.title: Which button takes the lift from the Art Centre to the Sports Centre?
media.context: The Other Side of Zero. Concept video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea. It ends when Keeko raises a hand with a doubt. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: The lift in the building has its Art Centre on one floor and its Sports Centre higher up. MATHEMATICAL IMAGE REQUIREMENT
Teaching purpose: Show that going from Floor −2 to Floor −1 needs a button of +1, which is target − start.

Composition: Flat, friendly educational illustration for a Class 6 maths lesson: plain white background, thin uniform dark outlines (#2B2B2B), flat fills with no shading and no gradients, clean sans-serif labels in plain classroom English a child can read aloud. Colour-blind-safe colours: #009E73 for a positive/first idea, #D55E00 for a negative/contrasting idea, #0072B2 for a first set or step, #E69F00 for a second set or step, #CC79A7 for the focus or highlight, #6B7280 for construction lines and for anything struck out. 16:9 landscape, 1456 by 816 pixels. Keep it uncluttered: one main idea only, at most three objects or groups, generous white space around everything, large readable labels, nothing decorative. One vertical lift shaft centred with a short upward arrow, wide white space either side.

Exact structure: One vertical shaft with 5 equal floor lines, evenly spaced, labelled +1, 0 (grey #6B7280 ground line), −1, −2, −3 top to bottom. A teal #0072B2 dot at floor −2 (start) and an amber #E69F00 dot at floor −1 (target). One reddish purple #CC79A7 upward arrow between them spanning exactly 1 floor. Exactly 5 floor lines, 2 dots, 1 arrow.

Visible text, exactly and only: start −2; target −1; +1; (−1) − (−2) = +1

Takeaway: Target minus start still gives the button, even below ground.

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students read a subtraction as finding what must be added to the smaller quantity to make it equal to the larger.
Students find the button to press between two floors as Target Floor − Starting Floor = Movement needed.
Students find the movement between floors when the start or the target is negative, and write it as a subtraction.
Students complete subtractions by finding the button that takes the lift from the starting floor to the target floor.

content.text:
The picture shows a mine, a place where minerals are extracted by digging into the rock. The truck is at the ground level, but the minerals are present both above and below the ground level. There is a fast moving lift which moves up and down in a mineshaft carrying people and ore.
Some of the levels are marked in the picture. The ground level is marked 0. Levels above the ground are marked by positive numbers and levels below the ground are marked by negative numbers. The number indicates how many metres above or below the ground level it is.
In the mine, just like in the Building of Fun: Starting Level + Movement = Target Level
For example, (+40) + (+60) = +100 and (−90) + (−55) = −145
Target Level − Starting Level = Movement needed
For example, (+40) − (−50) = +90 and (−90) − (+40) = −130
How many negative numbers are there? Bela's Building of Fun had only six floors above and five floors below. That is numbers −5 to +6. In the mine above, we have numbers from −200 to +180. But we can imagine larger buildings or mineshafts. Just as positive numbers +1, +2, +3, ... keep going up without an end, similarly, negative numbers −1, −2, −3, ... keep going down. Positive and negative numbers, with zero, are called integers. They go both ways from 0: ... −4, −3, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, ...

content.text:
1. Think first: a mine lift is at +40 m and goes 60 m up. Where does it stop? What if it were at −90 m and went 55 m further down?
2. It is the same rule as in Bela's building: Starting Level + Movement = Target Level, so (+40) + (+60) = +100 and (−90) + (−55) = −145.
3. And Target Level − Starting Level = Movement needed, so (+40) − (−50) = +90 and (−90) − (+40) = −130.

content.text:
To add and subtract even larger integers, we can imagine even larger lifts! In fact, we can imagine a lift that can extend forever upwards and forever downwards, starting from Level 0. There does not even have to be any building or mine around, just an 'infinite lift'!
We can use this imagination to add and subtract any integers we like.
For example, suppose we want to carry out the subtraction +2000 − (−200). We can imagine a lift with 2000 levels above the ground and 200 below the ground. Recall that, Target Level − Starting Level = Movement needed
To go from the Starting Floor −200 to the Target Floor +2000, we must press +2200 (+200 to get to zero, and then +2000 more after that to get to +2200). Therefore, (+2000) − (−200) = +2200.
Notice that (+2000) + (+200) is also +2200.

concepts.concept_name: Subtracting a negative is adding a positive

content.text:
Try evaluating the expressions by similarly drawing or imagining a suitable lift: a. −125 + (−30)  b. +105 − (−55)  c. +105 + (+55)  d. +80 − (−150)  e. +80 + (+150)  f. −99 − (−200)  g. −99 + (+200)  h. +1500 − (−1500)
In the above example, we saw that +2000 − (−200) = +2000 + (+200) = +2200. In other words, subtracting a negative number is the same as adding the corresponding positive number. That is, we can replace subtraction of a negative number by addition of a positive number!
In the other exercises that you did above, did you notice that subtracting a negative number was the same as adding the corresponding positive number?

concepts.concept_name: The lift is a number line

content.text:
Math Talk: Take a look at the 'infinite lift' above. Does it remind you of a number line? In what ways?
The 'infinite lift' we saw above looked very much like a number line, didn't it? In fact, if we rotate it by 90°, it basically becomes a number line. It also tells us how to complete the number ray to a number line, answering the question that we had asked at the beginning of the chapter. To the left of 0 are the negative numbers −1, −2, −3, ...
Usually we drop the '+' sign on positive numbers and simply write them as 1, 2, 3, ...
Instead of traveling along the number line using a lift, we can simply imagine walking on it. To the right is the positive (forward) direction, and to the left is the negative (backward) direction.
Smaller numbers are now to the left of bigger numbers and bigger numbers are to the right of smaller numbers. So, 2 < 5; −3 < 2; and −5 < −3.

content.text:
If, from 5 you wish to go over to 9, how far must you travel along the number line?
You must travel 4 steps. That is why 5 + 4 = 9.
(Remember: Starting Number + Movement = Target Number)
The corresponding subtraction statement is 9 − 5 = 4.
(Remember: Target Number − Starting Number = Movement needed)
Now, from 9, if you wish to go to 3, how much must you travel along the number line?
You must move 6 steps backward, i.e., you must move −6. Hence, we write 9 + (−6) = 3.
The corresponding subtraction statement is 3 − 9 = −6.
Now, from 3, if you wish to go to −2, how far must you travel?
You must travel −5 steps, i.e., 5 steps backward. Thus, 3 + (−5) = −2. The corresponding subtraction statement is: −2 − 3 = −5.

content.text:
1. Think first: from 5 you want to reach 9. How many steps do you take, and in which direction?
2. Four steps forward: 5 + 4 = 9, and 9 − 5 = 4. From 9 to 3 you go six steps backward, which is −6, so 9 + (−6) = 3 and 3 − 9 = −6.
3. From 3 to −2 you go five steps backward: 3 + (−5) = −2 and (−2) − 3 = −5. In every case Starting Number + Movement = Target Number.

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students see that rotating the endless lift by 90° gives a number line, and say how the two are alike.
Students find how far and in which direction to move from one number to another on the number line, and write the matching addition and subtraction.
Students mark positive and negative numbers, compare them on the line and walk from one number to another to complete sums and differences.

media.description: Two pairs of numbers are compared by their places on the number line. The number further to the right is the greater one, and the movement between them confirms it.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: on the number line, the number further to the right is the greater one. Watch for students who think negative three is greater because three is bigger than two.

media.title: What do six sums and differences of integers come to?
media.context: The Other Side of Zero. Question video: one question from the book, solved step by step by the method of the book's solved example. It opens only after the student has tried the question. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: Six sums and take aways of positive and negative numbers are worked as walks on the number line. The sums start at the first number and move by the sign of the second. The take aways are read as the movement from the second number to the first.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: a sum is a walk from the first number, and a take away a - b is the movement from b to a on the number line. Watch for students who think subtracting always makes a number smaller.

final_answer.spoken: negative five, zero, ten, negative ten, fourteen and two

maths_rules: a sum: start at the first number, a positive second number moves right, a negative one moves left
a take away x - y is the movement from y to x (target - start)
a. -5 + 0: no move, stay at -5
b. 7 + (-7): 7 steps left from 7 reaches 0
c. -10 + 20: 10 steps right to 0, then 10 more, reaches 10
d. 10 - 20: movement from 20 to 10 is 10 steps left, -10
e. 7 - (-7): movement from -7 to 7 is 7 + 7 = 14 steps right, +14
f. -8 - (-10): movement from -10 to -8 is 2 steps right, +2

concepts.concept_name: Adding on an unmarked number line

content.text:
Just as you can do additions, subtractions and comparisons with small numbers using the number line above, you can also do them with large numbers by imagining an 'infinite number line' or drawing an 'unmarked number line' as follows:
This line shows only the position of zero. Other numbers are not marked. It can be convenient to use this unmarked number line to add and subtract integers. You can show, or simply imagine, the scale of the number line and the positions of numbers on it.
For example, this unmarked number line (UNL) shows the addition problem: 85 + (−60) = ?
We then can visualise that 85 + (−60) = 25

content.text:
1. Think first: how would you find 85 + (−60) without drawing every number from 0 to 85?
2. Draw a line that shows only 0, mark 85, then move 60 to the left. The scale is imagined.
3. You land at 25, so 85 + (−60) = 25. A rough line is enough when only the movement matters.

content.text:
The following UNL shows a subtraction problem which can also be written as a missing addend problem: (−100) − (+250) = ? or 250 + ? = −100.

concepts.concept_name: Subtraction becomes addition of the inverse

content.text:
Recall that Target Floor − Starting Floor = Movement needed, or Target Floor = Starting Floor + Movement needed
If we start at 2 and wish to go to −3, what is the movement needed?
First method: Looking at the number line, we see we need to move −5 (i.e., 5 in the backward direction). Therefore, −3 − 2 = −5. The movement needed is −5.
Second method: Break the journey from 2 to −3 into two parts. a. From 2 to 0, the movement is 0 − 2 = −2. b. From 0 to −3, the movement is −3 − 0 = −3.
The total movement is the sum of the two movements: −3 + (−2) = −5.
Look at the two coloured expressions. There is no subtraction in the second one!
In this way, we can always convert subtraction to addition. The number that is being subtracted can be replaced by its inverse and then added instead.
Similarly, a number that is being added can be replaced by its inverse and then subtracted. In this way, we can also always convert addition to subtraction.
Examples: a. (+7) − (+5) = (+7) + (−5)  b. (−3) − (+8) = (−3) + (−8)  c. (+8) − (−2) = (+8) + (+2)  d. (+6) − (−9) = (+6) + (+9)

content.text:
1. Think first: from 2 to −3 the movement needed is −3 − 2. Can you find the same movement in two steps that need no subtraction?
2. Go from 2 to 0, which is −2, and then from 0 to −3, which is −3. Together −3 + (−2) = −5.
3. So subtracting a number is the same as adding its inverse, and adding a number is the same as subtracting its inverse.

content.text:
In Bela's Building of Fun, the lift attendant is bored. To entertain himself, he keeps a box containing lots of positive (green) and negative (red) tokens. Each time he presses the '+' button, he takes a positive token from the box and puts it in his pocket. Similarly, each time he presses the '−' button, he takes a negative token and puts it in his pocket.
He starts on the ground floor (Floor 0) with an empty pocket. After one hour, he checks his pocket and finds 5 positive and 3 negative tokens. On which floor is he now?
He must have pressed '+' five times and '−' 3 times and (+5) + (−3) = +2. So, he is at Floor +2 now.
Here is another way to do the calculation.
A positive token and a negative token cancel each other, because the value of this pair of tokens together is zero. These two tokens in his pocket meant that he pressed '+' once and '−' once, respectively, and these cancel each other. We say that a positive and a negative token make a 'zero pair'. When you remove all the zero pairs, you are left with two positive tokens, so (+5) + (−3) = +2.
We can perform any such addition using tokens!

3 zero pairs cancel, leaving 2 positive tokens: +2.

content.text:
Example: Add +5 and −8.
From the picture, we see that we can remove five zero pairs, and we are then left with −3. Therefore (+5) + (−8) = −3.

content.text:
1. Think first: to add +5 and −8 with tokens, how many zero pairs can you find?
2. Put down 5 green and 8 red tokens. Remove five zero pairs, and three red tokens remain.
3. So (+5) + (−8) = −3. The sign of the answer is the colour of the tokens left over.

media.description: A lift attendant keeps a positive token for every plus press and a negative token for every minus press. Pairs of one positive and one negative token cancel, and the tokens left show his floor. Keeko doubts this and counts all eight tokens as the floor.

maths_rules: each plus press puts 1 positive token (+1) in the pocket; each minus press puts 1 negative token (−1)
5 positive and 3 negative tokens: (+5) + (−3)
1 positive and 1 negative token make a zero pair: (+1) + (−1) = 0
3 negative tokens match 3 positive tokens, giving 3 zero pairs; 5 − 3 = 2 positive tokens stay
(+5) + (−3) = +2, so he is on Floor +2
slip: 5 + 3 = 8 counts the tokens, but positive and negative tokens pull in opposite directions

content.text:
We have seen how to perform addition of integers with positive tokens and negative tokens. We can also perform subtraction using tokens!
Example: Let us subtract: (+5) − (+4). This is easy to do. From 5 positives take away 4 positives to see the result. (+5) − (+4) = +1
Example: Let us subtract: (−7) − (−5). (−7) − (−5) = −2
Is (−7) − (−5) the same as (−7) + (+5)?

content.text:
1. Think first: from 5 green tokens, take away 4 green tokens. What is left?
2. One green token is left, so (+5) − (+4) = +1. With red tokens, from 7 red take away 5 red and 2 red are left: (−7) − (−5) = −2.
3. Taking away 5 red tokens gives the same result as adding 5 green tokens: (−7) − (−5) and (−7) + (+5) are both −2.

concepts.concept_name: Not enough tokens: put in a zero pair

content.text:
Example: Let us subtract: (+5) − (+6). Put down 5 positives. But there are not enough tokens to take out 6 positives!
To get around this issue, we can put out an extra zero pair (a positive and a negative), knowing that this does not change the value of the set of tokens.
Now, we can take out 6 positives! See what is left: We conclude that (+5) − (+6) = −1.

1. Think first: you have 5 green tokens and must take away 6 green tokens. What can you do?
2. Put out an extra zero pair, one green and one red. The value stays the same, and now there are 6 green tokens to take.
3. Take them away and one red token is left, so (+5) − (+6) = −1.

Example: +4 − (−6). Start with 4 positives. We have to take out 6 negatives from these. But there are not enough negatives.
This is not a problem. We add some zero pairs as this does not change the value of the set of tokens.

Now we can take away 6 negatives:
Therefore, +4 − (−6) = +10.

3. So (+4) − (−6) = +10. Taking away a negative token gives a positive result.

concepts.concept_name: Pull it together and do it: Token Taker

content.text:
Take tokens away when there are enough.
When there are not enough, add zero pairs until there are; the value does not change.
Count the zero pairs added and read what is left.

media.description: Seven negative tokens are changed in two ways: five negative tokens are taken away, or five positive tokens are added. Both ways leave the same two negative tokens. Keeko thinks taking away must make a number smaller and adding must make it bigger, so they cannot match.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: taking away negative tokens gives the same value as adding the same number of positive tokens. Watch for students who think taking away always lowers a value.

10.2, page 18, Figure it Out 1: Try to subtract: −3 − (+5). How many zero pairs will you have to put in? What is the result?

concepts.concept_name: Credit goes up, debit goes down

content.text:
Suppose you open a bank account at your local bank with the ₹100 that you had been saving over the last month. Your bank balance therefore, starts at ₹100.
Then you make ₹60 at your job the next day and you deposit it in your account. This is shown in your bank passbook as a 'credit'.
Your new bank balance is ______.
The next day you pay your electric bill of ₹30 using your bank account. This is shown in your bank passbook as a 'debit'.
Your bank balance is now ______.

content.text:
1. Think first: you open an account with ₹100, add ₹60 the next day and pay a ₹30 bill the day after. What is the balance now?
2. The ₹60 deposited is a credit, so the balance is ₹160. The ₹30 paid is a debit, so the balance is now ₹130.
3. Credits behave like positive numbers and debits like negative numbers.

content.text:
The next day you make a major purchase for your business of ₹150. Again this is shown as a debit.
What is your bank balance now? ______ Is this possible?
Yes, some banks do allow your account balance to become negative, temporarily! Some banks also charge you an additional amount if your balance becomes negative, in the form of 'interest' or a 'fee'.
Your strategic large purchase the previous day allows you to make, ₹200 at your business the next day.
What is your balance now? ______
You can think of 'credits' as positive numbers and 'debits' as negative numbers. The total of all your credits (positive numbers) and debits (negative numbers) is your total bank account balance. This can be positive or negative!
In general, it is better to try to keep a positive balance in your bank account!

content.text:
1. Think first: your balance is ₹130 and you buy something for ₹150. Is that possible?
2. Some banks allow it for a while. The balance is 130 − 150 = −20, and a later credit of ₹200 brings it to −20 + 200 = 180.
3. The total of all credits (positive) and debits (negative) is the balance, which can be positive or negative. It is better to keep it positive.

content.text:
10.3, page 19, Figure it Out 1: Suppose you start with ₹0 in your bank account, and then you have credits of ₹30, ₹40, and ₹50, and debits of ₹40, ₹50, and ₹60. What is your bank account balance now?
1. (+30) + (+40) + (+50) − 40 − 50 − 60 = 120 − 150 = −30.
Answer: −₹30

content.text:
10.3, page 19, Figure it Out 2: Suppose you start with ₹0 in your bank account, and then you have debits of ₹1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, and 128, and then a single credit of ₹256. What is your bank account balance now?
1. Debits total 1+2+4+8+16+32+64+128 = 255.
2. 256 − 255 = +1.
Answer: ₹1

content.text:
10.3, page 19, Figure it Out 3: Why is it generally better to try and maintain a positive balance in your bank account? What are circumstances under which it may be worthwhile to temporarily have a negative balance?
Answer: Open-ended. A positive balance avoids fees or interest the bank may charge on a negative balance; a short negative balance may be worthwhile to make an important purchase that earns more soon after (as in the business example).

content.text:
We measure the height of geographical features like mountains, plateaus, and deserts from 'sea level'. The height at sea level is 0m. Heights above sea level are represented using positive numbers and heights below sea level are represented using negative numbers.
Figure it Out
1. Looking at the geographical cross section, fill in the respective heights: a. ___ b. ___ c. ___ d. ___ e. ___ f. ___ g. ___
Teacher's Note: Ask what a geographical cross section is by showing the figure in this page. It is like imagining a vertical slice taken out at some location on the Earth. This is what would be seen from a side view. Discuss the notion of 'sea level' for measuring heights and depths in geography.
2. Which is the highest point in this geographical cross section? Which is the lowest point?
3. Can you write the points A, B, ..., G in a sequence of decreasing order of heights? Can you write the points in a sequence of increasing order of heights?
4. What is the highest point above sea level on Earth? What is its height?
5. What is the lowest point with respect to sea level on land or on the ocean floor? What is its height? (This height should be negative).

content.text:
1. Think first: a mountain top is above the sea and the ocean floor is below it. How could one scale measure both?
2. Height is measured from sea level, which is 0 m. Heights above sea level are positive and heights below are negative.
3. A point at −1200 m is lower than a point at −200 m, so the deeper point is the smaller number.

content.text:
During summer time you would have heard in the news that there is a 'heat wave'. What do you think will be the temperature during the summer when you feel very hot? In the winter we have cooler or colder temperatures.
What has been the maximum temperature during the summer and the minimum temperature during the winter last year in your area? Find out.
When we measure temperature, we use Celsius as the unit of measure (°C). The thermometers below are showing 40°C and 15°C temperatures.

content.text:
1. Think first: a thermometer shows 40 °C on a hot day and 15 °C on a cool one. Can it show a number below 0?
2. Yes. On a very cold day the temperature can be −4 °C, which is 4 degrees below the freezing point of water.
3. Colder means a smaller number: −4 °C is colder than −2 °C, and every temperature below 0 is colder than every temperature above 0.

content.text:
Worked example: Look at the two thermometers showing 40 °C and 15 °C. How could a thermometer show a temperature below 0 °C, and what would it mean?
1. The scale of the thermometer continues below 0 °C.
2. A reading below 0 °C is a negative number: the temperature is below the freezing point of water.
Answer: A thermometer can show a negative reading below 0 °C, for example −4 °C, which is colder than 0 °C.

media.title: How do we order the points from highest to lowest?
media.context: The Other Side of Zero. Question video: one question from the book, solved step by step by the method of the book's solved example. It opens only after the student has tried the question. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: The seven heights of the cross section are sorted into a list from the greatest to the least, and then the list is turned around. Positive heights come first, then the negative ones with the one nearest to zero first. The slip of putting minus twelve hundred before minus two hundred is shown.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: a decreasing order starts with the greatest number, and among negative numbers the one nearest to zero is the greater. Watch for students who put minus twelve hundred above minus two hundred because twelve hundred is the bigger number.
media.instructions_for_student: Try the question in your notebook first. Then watch; when the video says think and tell, say your answer.

content.text:
There is something special about the numbers in these two grids. Let us explore what that is.
Top row: 4 + (−1) + (−3) = 0 ; 5 + (−3) + (−5) = ____
Bottom row: (−1) + (−1) + 2 = 0 ; (−8) + (−2) + 7 = ____
Left column: 4 + (−3) + (−1) = 0 ; 5 + 0 + (−8) = ____
Right column: (−3) + 1 + 2 = 0 ; (−5) + (−5) + 7 = ____
In each grid, the numbers in each of the two rows (the top row and the bottom row) and the numbers in each of the two columns (the leftmost column and the rightmost column) add up to give the same number. We shall call this sum as the 'border sum'. The border sum of the first grid is '0'.
Figure it Out

content.text:
1. Think first: in the first grid the top row 4, −1, −3 adds to 0. Will the bottom row also give 0?
2. Yes: top row 4 + (−1) + (−3) = 0 and bottom row (−1) + (−1) + 2 = 0. The left column and the right column also give 0.
3. The common sum of the two rows and two columns is the border sum. Check the second grid and see whether the four sums match.

content.text:
1. Think first: a side has 4, −1 and a blank, and the border sum is 0. What goes in the blank?
2. The three numbers must add to the border sum. 4 + (−1) = 3, and 3 + (−3) = 0, so the blank is −3.
3. The corner numbers belong to two sides, so choose them first, then the middle numbers follow. If the corners can be changed, the grid can be filled in more than one way.

A corner is shared by two sides, so many grids can be filled in more than one way.

1. Think first: you circle any number, strike out its row and column, and repeat. Will the sum depend on what you choose?
2. In the book's example the circled numbers are −1, 9, −7 and −2, and they add to −1.
3. Play again with other choices and add each time. The sum comes out the same.

Worked example: Below is a grid having some numbers. Follow the steps until no number is left: circle any number; strike out the row and column of the chosen number; circle any unstruck number; repeat. When there are no more unstruck numbers, STOP. Add the circled numbers. Grid: row1 3, 4, 0, 9; row2 −2, −1, −5, 4; row3 1, 2, −2, 7; row4 −7, −6, −10, −1. Example in book: circled numbers −1, 9, −7, −2 add to −1.

2. Repeat with an unstruck number until 4 numbers are circled
3. Add circled numbers: −1 + 9 + (−7) + (−2) = −1

content.text:
1. Think first: look along row 2. Each number is 5 less than the number above it in row 1. Is there a pattern like this in every row?
2. Every number in the grid is a row number plus a column number: row 2 is the first row with 5 taken off, row 3 is the first row with 2 taken off, and row 4 is the first row with 10 taken off.
3. Each circle uses one row and one column exactly once, so the total is the sum of the first row, 3 + 4 + 0 + 9 = 16, plus 0 − 5 − 2 − 10 = −17, which is −1 every time. The magic is in the way the numbers are arranged.

content.text:
1. Think first: which integers lie between −4 and 4? Do −4 and 4 count?
2. Between −4 and 4 are −3, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3. The two ends are not between themselves.
3. When both numbers are negative, such as −8 and −15, the integers between them are −14 up to −9, listed from the smallest to the greatest.

concepts.concept_name: Years before and after the year 1

content.text:
1. Think first: the year after 1 BCE is 1 CE. Is there a year 0 in between?
2. No. The years run ..., 2 BCE, 1 BCE, 1 CE, 2 CE, ... So going back 3 years from 2 CE gives 2 BCE: 1 CE, then 1 BCE, then 2 BCE.
3. As a calculation, 2 − 3 = −1, and the first negative year, −1, is called 2 BCE. One extra step is needed because the year 0 is missing.

3. As a calculation, 2 − 3 = −1, and the first negative year, −1, is called 2 BCE. One extra step is needed because the year 0 is missing.

No. The years run ..., 2 BCE, 1 BCE, 1 CE, 2 CE, ... So going back 3 years from 2 CE gives 2 BCE: 1 CE, then 1 BCE, then 2 BCE.
As a calculation, 2 − 3 = −1, and the first negative year, −1, is called 2 BCE. One extra step is needed because the year 0 is missing.

media.description: Four pairs of numbers sit on the number line, the smaller number on the left. media.description: Eight sums and differences are made from thirteen and eight with different signs. media.title: How do we find the missing numbers in a pattern?

media.description: Three number patterns with missing numbers are completed by finding the gap from each number to the next. One pattern has a steady gap, one is two patterns taking turns, and one has gaps that grow by one. The video breaks the slip of thinking every pattern needs the same gap each time.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: the gap from one number to the next, target minus start, shows the rule of a pattern. Watch for students who look for one steady gap in every sequence, or who only extend forwards when numbers are missing at the start.

media.title: Which cards bring the value close to minus thirty?
media.context: The Other Side of Zero. Question video: one question from the book, solved step by step by the method of the book's solved example. It opens only after the student has tried the question. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: Six cards with positive and negative numbers are joined by additions and subtractions to reach a value as close to minus thirty as possible. media.title: Can we tell the sign of an answer in advance?
media.context: The Other Side of Zero. Question video: one question from the book, solved step by step by the method of the book's solved example. It opens only after the student has tried the question. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: Six cases of adding or taking away positive and negative numbers are sorted by the signs of the numbers involved. Every subtraction is turned into adding the additive inverse, and the cases with the same signs have a fixed sign while the cases with different signs depend on the numbers. The video breaks the slip of thinking that taking away always makes a number smaller.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: turn each subtraction into an addition, then ask whether the two numbers have the same sign or different signs. Watch for students who think that taking away a negative number must give a negative answer.
media.instructions_for_student: Try the question in your notebook first. Then watch; when the video says think and tell, say your answer.

media.title: What is the value of this string of tokens?
media.context: The Other Side of Zero. Question video: one question from the book, solved step by step by the method of the book's solved example. It opens only after the student has tried the question. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: A string of one hundred tokens repeats three green tokens and then two red tokens. Zero pairs are cancelled in one block of five, and the value of one block is multiplied by the number of blocks. The video breaks the slip of thinking that the value of a string is just the number of its tokens.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: cancel the zero pairs in one repeating block, then count the blocks. Watch for students who give the number of tokens as the value, forgetting that a red token is worth minus one.
media.instructions_for_student: Try the question in your notebook first. Then watch; when the video says think and tell, say your answer.

content.text:
Like general fractions, general integers (including zero and the negative numbers) were first conceived of and used in Asia, thousands of years ago, before they eventually spread across the world in more modern times.
The first known instances of the use of negative numbers occurred in the context of accounting. In one of China's most important mathematical works, The Nine Chapters on Mathematical Art (Jiuzhang Suanshu), which was completed by the first or second century CE, positive and negative numbers were represented using red and black rods, much like the way we represented them using green and red tokens!
There was a strong culture of accountancy also in India in ancient times. The concept of credit and debit was written about extensively by Kautilya in his Arthashastra (c. 300 BCE), including the recognition that an account balance could be negative. The explicit use of negative numbers in the context of accounting is seen in a number of ancient Indian works, including in the Bakshali manuscript from around the year 300 CE, where a negative number was written using a special symbol placed after the number (rather than before the number as we do today).
The first general treatment of positive numbers, negative numbers, and zero, all on an equal footing as equally-valid numbers on which one can perform the basic operations of addition, subtraction, multiplication, and even division, was given by Brahmagupta in his Brahma-sphuta-siddhanta in the year 628 CE. Brahmagupta gave clear and explicit rules for operations on all numbers, positive, negative, and zero, that essentially formed the modern way of understanding these numbers that we still use today!

content.text:
Some of Brahmagupta's key rules for addition and subtraction of positive numbers, negative numbers and zero are given below:
Brahmagupta's Rules for Addition (Brahma-sphuta-siddhanta 18.30, 628 CE)
1. The sum of two positives is positive (e.g., 2 + 3 = 5).
2. The sum of two negatives is negative. To add two negatives, add the numbers (without the signs), and then place a minus sign to obtain the result (e.g., (−2) + (−3) = −5).
3. To add a positive number and a negative number, subtract the smaller number (without the sign) from the greater number (without the sign), and place the sign of the greater number to obtain the result (e.g., −5 + 3 = −2, 2 + (−3) = −1 and −3 + 5 = 2).
4. The sum of a number and its inverse is zero (e.g., 2 + (−2) = 0).
5. The sum of any number and zero is the same number (e.g., −2 + 0 = −2 and 0 + 0 = 0).

content.text:
1. Think first: in Bela's lift, 2 floors up and then 3 floors up is 5 floors up. Which rule is that?
2. Rule 1: two positives give a positive, 2 + 3 = 5. Rule 2: add two negatives without the signs and put a minus, (−2) + (−3) = −5.
3. Rule 3: for one positive and one negative, subtract the smaller from the greater and take the sign of the greater, so 5 + (−8) = −3. Rule 4: a number plus its inverse is 0. Rule 5: adding 0 changes nothing.

content.text:
Brahmagupta's Rules for Subtraction (Brahma-sphuta-siddhanta 18.31-18.32)
1. If a smaller positive is subtracted from a larger positive, the result is positive (e.g., 3 − 2 = 1).
2. If a larger positive is subtracted from a smaller positive, the result is negative (e.g., 2 − 3 = −1).
3. Subtracting a negative number is the same as adding the corresponding positive number (e.g., 2 − (−3) = 2 + 3).
4. Subtracting a number from itself gives zero (e.g., 2 − 2 = 0 and −2 − (−2) = 0).
5. Subtracting zero from a number gives the same number (e.g., −2 − 0 = −2 and 0 − 0 = 0). Subtracting a number from zero gives the number's inverse (e.g., 0 − (−2) = 2).
Once you understand Brahmagupta's rules, you can do addition and subtraction with any numbers whatsoever, positive, negative, and zero!
Figure it Out

content.text:
1. Think first: what do you get from 2 − (−3) on the number line? From −3 to 2 you move 5 steps right.
2. Rule 3: subtracting a negative number is the same as adding the corresponding positive number, so 2 − (−3) = 2 + 3 = 5. Rule 4: a number minus itself is 0.
3. Rule 1: 3 − 2 = 1. Rule 2: 2 − 3 = −1. Rule 5: subtracting 0 changes nothing, and 0 − 2 = −2, the inverse of 2.

media.title: Can a lift explain all ten rules?
media.context: The Other Side of Zero. Question video: one question from the book, solved step by step by the method of the book's solved example. It opens only after the student has tried the question. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: The five rules for adding and the five rules for subtracting in the book are each explained as a movement of the lift between floors. Addition is starting floor plus movement, and subtraction is the movement from one floor to another. The video breaks the slip of thinking that subtraction is a separate idea with no picture.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: every rule is a movement of the lift, with starting floor plus movement giving the target floor. Watch for students who memorise the rules without seeing the movement, especially for taking away a negative number.
media.instructions_for_student: Try the question in your notebook first. Then watch; when the video says think and tell, say your answer.

concepts.concept_name: Rolling a positive and a negative die

content.text:
This is a two player game. Each player has 1 pawn. Both players start at 0. Players can reach either −50 or +50 to win but need not decide or fix this before or during play.
Each player rolls two dice at a time. One dice has numbers from +1 to +6 and the other dice has numbers from −1 to −6.
After each roll of the two dice, the player can add or subtract them in any order and then move the steps that indicate the result. A positive result means moving towards +50 and a negative result means moving towards −50.

content.text:
1. Think first: you roll +4 and −5. Adding gives −1. What does subtracting give, in each order?
2. (+4) + (−5) = −1, (+4) − (−5) = 9 and (−5) − (+4) = −9. A positive result moves you towards +50 and a negative result moves you towards −50.
3. Choose the result that helps most; the winner is the first to reach +50 or −50.

content.text:
Worked example: Two-player game. Each player has 1 pawn; both start at 0. Players can reach either −50 or +50 to win but need not decide this before or during play. Each player rolls two dice at a time, one with +1 to +6 and the other with −1 to −6. After each roll the player can add or subtract them in any order and then move the steps that indicate the result. A positive result means moving towards +50 and a negative result towards −50.
1. Roll the +1 to +6 die and the −1 to −6 die.
2. Add or subtract the two numbers in either order.
3. Move that many steps: towards +50 if positive, towards −50 if negative.
Answer: Play the game: the first pawn to reach +50 or −50 wins.

concepts.concept_name: The other side of zero, in one page

content.text:
There are numbers that are less than zero. They are written with a '−' sign in front of them (e.g., −2), and are called negative numbers. They lie to the left of zero on the number line.
The numbers ..., −4, −3, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, ... are called integers. The numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, ... are called positive integers and the numbers ..., −4, −3, −2, −1 are called negative integers. Zero (0) is neither positive nor negative.
Every given number has another number associated to it which when added to the given number gives zero. This is called the additive inverse of the number. For example, the additive inverse of 7 is −7 and the additive inverse of −543 is 543.

content.text:
1. Think first: if someone asks you what the other side of zero holds, what will you say?
2. Numbers less than zero are negative numbers; with the positive numbers and zero they make the integers, and every integer has an additive inverse.
3. Starting Position + Movement = Target Position, and subtracting an integer is adding its inverse. Smaller numbers lie to the left of larger ones, and credits, debits, heights and temperatures all use integers.

objectives.objective_text: Students point out the floors that lie below the ground in the Building of Fun and say what the ground floor holds.
Students read pressing '+' as going up, pressing '−' as going down, and write four floors up and three floors down as +4 and −3.
Students number every floor of the Building of Fun from the ground floor, and explain why the ground floor is Floor 0.
Students say which floor numbers are positive, which are negative and which is neither, and match a button press to a floor.
Students write a move in the lift as Starting Floor + Movement = Target Floor, and find the target floor.
Students combine a run of '+' and '−' presses into one movement and write it as an addition.
Students cancel a press with the press of equal size in the other direction, and name the inverse of an integer.
Students press lift buttons from different floors, read the target floor and write the addition.
Students give the floor number of each child and decide who is on the lowest floor.
Students write < or > between two integers by asking which floor is higher, including two negative floors.
Students compare integers with < and >, fill in the numbers on a vertical line of floors and mark floors on it.
Students read a subtraction as finding what must be added to the smaller quantity to make it equal to the larger.
Students find the button to press between two floors as Target Floor − Starting Floor = Movement needed.
Students find the movement between floors when the start or the target is negative, and write it as a subtraction.
Students complete subtractions by finding the button that takes the lift from the starting floor to the target floor.
Students add and subtract levels in a mine, where metres above the ground are positive and metres below are negative.
Students imagine a lift that runs without end above and below the ground and use it to find +2000 − (−200).
Students notice that subtracting a negative number gives the same result as adding the matching positive number.
Students fill in missing movements and evaluate sums and differences by thinking of the mineshaft.
Students see that rotating the endless lift by 90° gives a number line, and say how the two are alike.
Students find how far and in which direction to move from one number to another on the number line, and write the matching addition and subtraction.
Students mark positive and negative numbers, compare them on the line and walk from one number to another to complete sums and differences.
Students show a sum of large integers on an unmarked number line and read off the result.
Students show a subtraction as a missing addend on an unmarked number line and read off the movement.
Students rewrite a subtraction as the addition of the inverse, and check it on the number line.
Students rewrite subtractions as additions of the inverse and say what each pair of expressions shares.
Students read the lift attendant's tokens as a floor number by counting positive and negative tokens.
Students add two integers of different sign by cancelling zero pairs and reading what is left.
Students add integers by putting down green and red tokens, cancelling zero pairs and reading the floor.
Students subtract by taking tokens off the board when there are enough of that kind.
Students subtract a larger positive from a smaller positive by adding a zero pair first.
Students subtract a negative number by adding enough zero pairs and taking the red tokens away.
Students subtract integers with tokens, adding zero pairs when they need more tokens to take away.
Students follow a savings account and say how each credit and each debit changes the balance.
Students find a balance after a debit larger than the balance, and say that it is a negative balance.
Students total a list of credits and debits to find a balance and say what a negative balance means.
Students read heights above and below sea level as positive and negative numbers and compare them.
Students read a thermometer in °C, say what a negative reading means, and compare temperatures.
Students fill in heights from a cross section, order them, name the highest and lowest places on Earth and match temperatures to times.
Students add the four sides of a hollow grid and see that all four sums are the same.
Students find the missing number of a side from the border sum and the two numbers already given.
Students fill hollow grids to reach a border sum, find more than one filling and make a puzzle.
Students play the circle and strike out game on a grid and add the numbers they circled.
Students explain that each circled number comes from a different row and column, so the sum is fixed.
Students play the game on new grids, say what is special about them and make a grid of their own.
Students list all the integers between two given integers in increasing order, leaving out the ends.
Students count years back from a CE year to a BCE year and say why there is no year 0.
Students solve the second set of Figure it Out puzzles on integers between, sums, dice, years, sequences, cards and a string of tokens.
Students tell where negative numbers were first used and who gave the first general treatment of them.
Students state the five rules for adding integers and check each one with the lift.
Students state the five rules for subtracting integers and check each one on the number line.
Students explain each of Brahmagupta's rules with the lift or the number line and give their own example for each.
Students roll one die of +1 to +6 and one of −1 to −6, then add or subtract in either order to get a move.
Students play the two-dice integer game against a friend and choose the best move on each roll.
Students recall what integers are and how adding and subtracting them follow one set of rules.
